t: 3706. Maximum Distance Between Unequal Words in Array II
o: We want the farthest index pair holding different strings. Key observation: an optimal pair almost always involves an endpoint. If `words[0] != words[n-1]`, the whole array works (distance n). Otherwise both endpoints equal some word w; the best pair uses the first index holding a non-w word paired with the last index, or vice versa. With n up to 1e5, O(n²) pairing is too slow, but the endpoint argument gives O(n).
k: If the first and last words differ, the answer is simply n.
Otherwise scan inward from both ends to find the outermost indices whose word differs from words[0].

a.i: Compare the two endpoints first. If equal, the farthest valid partner for index 0 is the last differing-from-the-right index, and for index n-1 it is the first differing-from-the-left index; take the better of the two distances.
s: Advance i from 0 until words[i] != words[0]; if none exists return 0.
Move j from n-1 down until words[j] != words[n-1].
a.t: O(n) — at most two linear scans

a.n: Approach 2: Brute Force with Early Exit
a.i: Try all pairs from the widest spans downward; the first unequal pair found at each span gives the answer. Simple but quadratic in the worst case (all words equal).
s: For each i, check words[i] != words[i+gap]; if so return gap+1.
a.t: O(n²) worst case — all pairs scanned when the answer is 0

w: Always present the endpoint-scan solution; brute force only as a stepping stone. Pitfall: returning 0 correctly when every word is identical (guard the left scan). Follow-up: what if distance were defined as j - i instead?
